newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: INSIDER TRADING PROBES UP IN 97 - DUTCH REGULATOR.
newsitem.headline: INSIDER TRADING PROBES UP IN 97 - DUTCH REGULATOR.

text.p: The Dutch securities sector regulator on Thursday expressed concern at the ability of Dutch justice authorities to cope with a mushrooming number of insider trading cases, which could this year double 1996's total.
Presenting the 1996 annual report of the Netherlands Securities Board STE, chairman Francis Loudon said the number of suspected cases investigated had risen sharply in 1997.

Amplifying on his comments STE director Bert Canneman said, "If we carry on at this rate (of passing dossiers onto the public prosecutor) it is evident that the prosecuting authorities will run into difficulties."
"So far this year we have rounded off 11 investigations into possible insider trading, of which three have been reported (to the public prosecutor)," Loudon said.
A further six investigations were still underway, he said, adding that the total to date for 1997 was well up on the 14 probes mounted by the STE for the whole of 1996.
Three of these cases were also passed on to the justice authorities.

Loudon said that the explosion in stock market activity was the main motor behind the uptrend in suspected insider trading and the STE was concerned about the ability of justice authorities to cope with the increase.
Both the public prosecutor and the courts were experiencing bottlenecks in dealing with cases, he said.

Effective January 1 this year, the securities sector watchdog has taken over the compliance and enforcement role of the newly-merged Amsterdam stock and options exchanges, which were previously self-regulating.
The switch to an independent regulatory body was due in part to the huge expansion in securities dealing, market internationalisation and the commercialisation of Amsterdam's bourses, Loudon said.
-- Lien van der Leij, Amsterdam newsroom +31 20 504 5000.
